transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: July 20, 1969. At 1:44 in the afternoon, Eastern time, the lunar module Eagle undocks from Columbia, with Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin aboard.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Michael Collins stays behind, orbiting the Moon alone.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: At 4:05 PM, Eagle's descent engine fires for the powered descent to the surface.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Minutes later, the guidance computer throws a 1202 program alarm. Mission control decides it is safe to keep going.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The planned landing spot is strewn with boulders, so Armstrong takes manual control and flies on, looking for flat ground, while the fuel runs low.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: At 4:17 PM, Eagle touches down in the Sea of Tranquility. The Eagle has landed.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: That night, at 10:56 PM, Armstrong steps onto the Moon: one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: About twenty minutes later, Aldrin joins him on the surface.

widgets.claim: A 1202 program alarm hit Eagle's guidance computer during descent, and mission control decided it was safe to continue.
widgets.speaker: Narrator
widgets.context: The sources agree that Apollo 11's guidance computer gave 1202 (and 1201) alarms during descent. Mission Control, advised by Garman and Bales, judged them a non-critical overload and let the landing continue.
widgets.source: T apollo 11 1201 1202 guidance computer restarts · spacedaily.com
widgets.counter: The call was made by specific controllers (Garman, Bales, Kranz), with a go/no-go each time the alarm recurred. The sources don't give exact timing.

sources.title: T apollo 11 1201 1202 guidance computer restarts · spacedaily.com

widgets.headline: 1202 alarm hit the computer, but Mission Control said go

widgets.claim: Armstrong took manual control to avoid a boulder-strewn landing area and flew on while fuel ran low.
widgets.speaker: Narrator
widgets.context: Sources agree Armstrong took (semi-)manual control to avoid a boulder-strewn area and craters, and searched for a landing site while fuel was low. Quoted fuel margins vary: about 25 seconds at landing, 60 seconds, or 2 minutes at takeover.
widgets.counter: Fuel figures differ by source and moment. Control was semi-manual (autopilot-assisted), and the "fuel" was a margin estimate, not an emergency.

answers.question: How much fuel was left when Eagle touched down?
answers.text: The episode doesn't say how much fuel was left at touchdown. It only says that during the manual flight to find flat ground, "the fuel runs low." No amount is given so far, and I can't see later in the episode.

answers.question: Why did the Moonwalk wait until that night?
answers.text: The episode hasn't explained the wait yet. It only shows touchdown at 4:17 PM and the first step at 10:56 PM, about six and a half hours later. From general knowledge, Apollo crews had a long set of post-landing checks and rest before going outside, but that isn't covered in what we've watched so far.

answers.question: What was the 1202 alarm, and why was it safe to keep going?
answers.text: The transcript only says the guidance computer threw a 1202 program alarm minutes after the descent engine fired, and that mission control decided it was safe to keep going. It doesn't explain the alarm or the reasoning yet. From a web search (spacedaily.com), the 1202 alarm signaled that the computer's executive routine had more jobs requesting processing than it could handle with its limited temporary memory. Controllers judged it safe because the alarms were intermittent and the computer recovered between them while still performing its essential guidance functions.

sources.title: T apollo 11 1201 1202 guidance computer restarts · spacedaily.com

answers.question: Why did Armstrong have to fly Eagle manually?
answers.text: The narrator says the planned landing spot was strewn with boulders, so Armstrong took manual control to look for flat ground. Fuel was running low while he did it. The transcript so far doesn't say whether the 1202 alarm played any part in that decision.

answers.question: What was Michael Collins doing while the others landed?
answers.text: So far the episode says Michael Collins stayed behind in orbit around the Moon, alone, while Armstrong and Aldrin undocked in the lunar module Eagle. It hasn't covered the landing yet, so I can't say what he was doing during it.
